The slopes of Lha ri mo in Grom pa. Śākya brtson ’grus was a scholar of the eleventh century, as can be inferred from other translation colophons, according to which he translated the *Abhiṣekanirukti* (Toh. 2477) and a...
The *Mahāmāyāsādhana* (Toh.
1626) together with Avadhūtipā (= Advayavajra), who lived from 1007/1010 to 1085/1088, and the *Mahāyānaviṃśati* (Toh. 2248).

Upon seeing the title *Vajraḍākottara* in the Kanjur, one would expect to find a work quite distinct from the *Vajraḍāka* itself; however, it has turned out to consist...
It consists almost entirely of extracts from the *Vajraḍāka* itself:
Chapter 1 = *Vajraḍāka*, Chapter 1;
Chapter 2 = *Vajraḍāka*, Chapter 2.
Paṭala 3 = the first part of Vajraḍāka Paṭala 3, with a deviation at the end;
Paṭala 12 = Vajraḍāka Paṭala 12 (Vajraḍākasādhanam);
Paṭala 14 (the last) = the first part of Vajraḍāka Paṭala 19 (Mātṛmaṇḍalam).
Paṭalas 4–11 and 13 are extremely short (pp. 263,7–266,2). I have not identified their provenance. I do not recall them in the *Vajraḍāka*, though I have not examined the text thoroughly.
The thirteenth paṭala contains certain material found in the eighteenth paṭala of the *Vajraḍāka*.
This circumstance is reflected in the colophons. With the exception of those for the third and the final (fourteenth) paṭalas, all others refer to the text simply as the [title of the tantra].

The *Vajraḍākamahātantra*. Chapter Three states that it is the *rDo rje mkha' 'gro ma'i rgyud chen po* (*Vajraḍākinīmahātantra*). However, this is likely the result of an error in which a scribe wrote "mkha' 'gro ma" (ḍākinī) instead of the less [common] term.
The common ḍākinī. The colophon of the fourteenth chapter calls the text the *Vajraḍākinī-hṛdaya*.
The colophon of the entire work, which follows immediately, calls it the *Vajraḍākinī-tantra-uttara-hṛdayasaṃgraha*.

The term *snying po* can render various Sanskrit words such as *hṛdaya*, *garbha*, *maṇḍa*, or *sāra*. However, the compound *snying po bsdus* likely renders *sārasaṃgraha*. Thus, the title in the colophon of the fourteenth [chapter] was probably: [End of sentence]

The title *Vajraḍākasāra* and the final colophon *Vajraḍākatantrōttarasārasaṃgraha* suggest that the intended meaning was "A compendium of the essential teachings [from the Vajraḍāka] as a supplement to..."

The text: *Vajraḍāka-nāmottaratantra* in the language of India; in the language of Tibet, *rDo rje mkha' 'gro zhes bya ba'i rgyud phyi ma*. "Vajraḍāka itself. The text: *rgya gar skad du ba dzra ḍā ka nā ma u tta ra tan tra | bod skad du rdo rje*... [continues with the Tibetan title].
The Explanatory Tantra called *Ḍākinī*. Homage to Maheśvara, the Supporter of the World!
In the secret, supreme, and delightful [rahasye parame ramye],
he dwells eternally as the sovereign of all.
Always abiding in the self of all;
the heroic being (*sattva*) consisting of all *ḍākinīs*.
Vajradāka, supreme bliss;
this is the self-arisen Blessed One.
He is the self-existent Blessed One;
he alone is the supreme deity.
The Blessed Ones, whose sphere of activity is the samaya, have emerged from the sound and form of the source (*sambhava*).
[The Blessed Ones are the domain of the conduct of the samaya.
They abide perfectly in the beginning, middle, and end;
they are difficult to find within the three worlds.
Difficult to find in the three worlds, abiding without beginning, end, or middle; it is neither passion nor free from passion.
Neither passion nor dispassion;
even the middle way is not apprehended.
This illusory seal of all women (sarvastrīmāyamudrā) is the supreme non-dual primordial wisdom.
Non-dual gnosis is supreme;
even those who do not practice will achieve accomplishment.
Through ease and joy, all gains are obtained;
the accomplishment of conduct throughout the entire expanse of space.
[The accomplishment of moving through all space:
She is renowned as a *ḍākinī* [she is known as a *ḍākinī*].
The universal seal of all variety,
the commitment that is entirely manifold.
The universal vow in every respect;
through the union with all ḍākinīs (*sarvaḍākinīsamāyoga*).
One becomes renowned as Vajraḍāka;
this is the visualization of the respective deity.
That very reality is the yoga beyond thought,
which arises definitively from empowerment;
it is the yoga of the nature of the reflected image.
The Great Yoga of Bodhicitta,
the Sovereign Lord of Yogis.
The Lord himself, the master of yoga;
bodhicitta is the vajra—
this bodhicitta is the vajra.
Because he is the nature of all Buddhas,
one should therefore strive with every effort.
Therefore, with every effort,
one should worship the one of manifold forms (*viśvarūpin*).
By the nature of mutual embrace,
he dwells pervading the various realms of beings.
[Pervading and abiding throughout the universe] | Buddhahood is my very self [the self is indeed all-buddhahood].
The yogin [should cultivate] the state of being a hero among sentient beings and one's own deity.
Through union with one's own presiding deity,
because he is the very self of the object to be accomplished, for that reason, the self itself is accomplished.
By this, the reality of all Buddhas and all powerful ones is [realized] as the state of the Universal Vajradhara.
By this very [means], Buddhahood and indeed the state of being a universal lord will be accomplished in this very life.
"And the state of being a holder of all vajras is accomplished in this very life," thus said the Blessed One, Śrī Vajrasattva.
The Hero,
the Blessed One, the Glorious Vajrasattva Tathāgata, spoke thus: [ity āha bhagavān śrīmān vajrasattvas tathāgataḥ].
The supreme bliss of the Vajra Ḍākinī,
the union of all ḍākinīs (*sarvaḍākasamāyoga*).
Vajraḍāka is supreme bliss;
the three realms in their entirety are all characterized by space.
Everything is like an illusion;
the entire triple world, without exception, has the characteristic of space.
All is indeed like an illusion, and space is also without characteristics;
this is what is seen and what is known.
It is seen and indeed touched;
everything is just like an illusion (*yathā māyā hi sarvataḥ*).
Those who abide among all beings are not apprehended at all;
indeed, they are not perceived.
The stability of the entire world;
by means of this mudrā, the yogin—
Wandering through the three worlds,
that delusion by which one becomes bound—
By those very things by which the deluded are bound, the wise are liberated;
the wise play with them here in this world.
The Buddhas are liberated through play;
sentient beings dwelling in the gathering places are born clearly manifest in various and diverse ways.
[The text diverges here:
Form is the Buddha Vairocana (*rūpaṃ vairocano buddhaḥ*).
Feeling is Vajrasūrya; perception is Padmanarteśvara.
[Padmanarteśvara is the designation];
likewise, Saṃskāra is Vajrarāja.
Consciousness is Vajrasattva,
the nature of all phenomena.
[He who possesses the nature of all forms]—
the renowned Vajradāka (Vajrasattva) is accomplished.
They are the sole great element;
they bestow all happiness.
[The manifester of all bliss: "Dust and the dustless are spoken of" (*virajaṃ rajam ity uktam*).
The very nature of Mahāmāyā is the earth that causes one to fall.
The earth element is indeed the "Causer of Falling," and likewise,
the water element is the "Slayer."
The fire element is Ākarṣaṇī;
likewise, the wind [element] is Gaurīśvarī.
[Wind is likewise Narteśvarī];
the nature of the space element is [the nature of the space element].
She is of the nature of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyāsvabhāvinī*),
by virtue of the nature of the five elements.
By way of the nature of the five elements,
that Vajra Leader resides there.
Through union with all that has arisen,
she is the blazing supreme ḍākinī.
[The Ḍākinī is supremely radiant.
The eyes are explained as Mohavajrā [the two eyes are called Mohavajrā].
Hearing is explained as Dveṣavajrā (Hatred Vajra);
likewise, greed is Mātsaryavajrā (Greed Vajra).
Likewise, the nose is Īrṣyāvajra;
the mouth is declared to be Rāgavajra.
Envy toward knowledge is Vajra-mātsarya;
it is the union with all women without exception.
The union of all sense bases—
Vajraḍāka, the supreme bliss.
Since seeing with the eyes and so forth are empty,
all these have the nature of emptiness.
All this has the nature of emptiness;
it is seen by the non-conceptual eye.
By that, one becomes free from hesitation;
these [phenomena] have the nature of space.
[*These have the nature of space].
(251,7) All minds have the nature of space, [with a mind that has the form of space].
When one possesses unimpeded cultivation,
non-conceptuality arises perfectly.
[Non-conceptualization arises. Thus, he spoke the sequence of the samādhi called "The Unimpeded and Meaningful Commitment of All Tathāgatas."
[Having performed the sequence of meditative absorption called *Sarvatathāgataniḥśaṅkāmoghasamaya* (The Unfailing Commitment of All Tathāgatas Free from Fear), he said:
"As long as those endowed with supreme knowledge remain within the state of cyclic existence,"

As long as they remain within cyclic existence, these supreme sages do not turn back from their peerless capacity to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings; for as long as they abide in saṃsāra, they are able to perform all incomparable deeds for the sake of beings without ever entering final nirvāṇa.

For this very reason, those sublime beings are always fearless within the noose of existence (*bhavapāśa*), and through their diligence, they constantly and swiftly act for the benefit of sentient beings without ever abandoning them. [ata eva satsattvā bhavapāśe sadābhayāḥ]

The first paṭala ends, 256,1: When the nature of the mind becomes stable, the mind wavers through the suffering of the beloved and proceeds further toward cessation; yet, when body and mind abide in bliss, awakening is attained.

"Having attained stability of body, speech, and mind, one shall obtain enlightenment; otherwise, there will be untimely death, and one will certainly fall into hell. O Blessed One, Vajradhara, Vajrasattva..."

Thus spoke the Tathāgata: [Thus said the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata. The Supreme Bliss of the Vajra-Ḍāka, the Union of All Ḍākinīs. [Sarvaḍākinīsamāyogavajraḍākaḥ paramaṃ sukham]
[Bliss].
From the Great Tantra of the Vajraḍākinī, this is the first chapter, which reveals the supreme reality and [describes] the engagement of cognition with its objects.
[The first chapter, titled "The Knowledge for Entering the Domain of the Contemplation of Supreme Reality," from the *Vajraḍāka-mahātantra*.]
Paṭala 2:
Then the Goddess, having again performed worship to the Blessed One and prostrated herself, spoke as follows: [atha bhagavatī devī punar api pūjāṃ kṛtvā...]

Having prostrated, he spoke thus: "The heart which thoroughly subdues the malevolent— *sarvaduṣṭaprabhañjanahṛdayam*— which subdues all malevolent ones who revile the teaching of all the Tathāgatas, and [subdues] the malevolent gods..."

"O Blessed One, please speak so that all such malicious beings may be tamed and disciplined, established in a state of peace, and remain without causing harm until they reach the heart of enlightenment. [Sarvaduṣṭāḥ sarvatathāgataśāsanadrohakāḥ]
All beings, including wicked gods and others, will be tamed and brought to discipline;
until they reach the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), they shall not act with wickedness. Then, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, sang this song:

He spoke thus: [Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the Vajras of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, uttered this song: First, one should place Vairocana; thereafter, one should recite the mantra.
[O, Vairocana, remain! All the Tathāgatas are free from attachment and shatter [it]; all the Bodhisattvas are weary of saṃsāra. Patala 2 ends: 261, 5. Thus it is said:
"The Tathāgatas are free from passion and destroy [it]; the Bodhisattvas are weary of cyclic existence."
They are the destroyers; thus, these are declared to be the accomplishers of all goddesses. These very kings of mantras have never appeared before, nor will they ever appear again.

"O Goddess, it has been thus declared: this King of Mantras, which shatters the passionlessness of all Tathāgatas and destroys the weariness of cyclic existence for all Bodhisattvas, is one that has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again."
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, the perfect accomplishment of the union with all the emanations of the ḍākinīs.
This is known as the *Sarvadaṅkinīmāyāsamāyoga*.
These are the rituals for all rituals from the *Vajraḍākamahātantra*, the great tantra of the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, and the *Māyā* [illusion].

This is the second chapter, the ritual procedure for the mantra of the great māyā’s miraculous manifestations, titled "The Procedure for the Expansion of All Activities" (*Sarvakarmaprasaravidhimahāmāyāvikurvaṇamantravidhipaṭala*).
Paṭala 3 begins: Then, the secret shall be spoken;
I shall speak it for the sake of brevity, not in detail. Through the equal union with the illusion of all things, [the activities...]

Equalizing all things (*sarvakarmasama*), the great illusory accomplishment of all (*sarvamāyāmahāsiddhiḥ*), and the complete attainment of all sovereignty (*sarvaiśvaryaṃ prasidhyati*). It causes vidyā to radiate forth; it is the transformative...
For the purpose of summoning the *bhūta*-demons, one should utter this supreme vidyā-mantra: To the north of the Himavat mountains, there is the Blessed One named Tshiba (Śiva), the Great Maso.
*Sobai adhamasi haṃ behima sehi masehi vati budzdza*.

One should consecrate it seven times with the explicit recitation [having performed the sevenfold consecration with this]. If it is placed upon the roof of the house, it will cause them to fall silent. *Vasahatolamiñja a ba*.
Svabhāvajano hi a | i se vijñatsaha inamanti indhana | ha abū ijabe nadinṇaṇi | dhataṃpahi mahāsvabhāvana nibuddhosi | rājakulakhaṇḍa | ṭanitajebuyibadha | tādhi ||

Na ta na | na maḥ si dha na | na maḥ pu pa dza dza pū da na | ma sa wa rā ṇe | ta dya da a re ma hā da ṇḍe da ja he du na he he svāhā | If one recites this mantra seven times over sesame seeds and scatters them [over the grains], what [will happen]?
Wild animals such as jackals and the like will not devour it, and the clouds will be dispersed;
[by performing this seven times with mantras and scattering sand,
one is not eaten by wild animals and the like, and through the warding off of clouds, this is the accomplishment].

*Ra tna ra ti | Oṃ ala la vara tsu li la tso ra ba ggha? ka na da sa pū mu ha ban dha mi svāhā |* If one recites this seven times over a four-finger-breadth piece of wood and fastens it to the right ear, it will paralyze thieves. (*Caturaṅulaṃ*)
Having recited the mantra seven times over a small piece of wood and placing it on the right ear, one effects the immobilization of thieves:
*ida si | ati ṇi dza ha a ka li lo hi hi | pi ṅg ale | ma me ga bha na i | a haṃ si la ā sa ri mi a ba ra bha ṇa i | a*.

One should not take earth dug up by the horns of an ox, but should empower it seven times with this [mantra] and [place it] in the forest.

One will not be harmed by anything— be it a wilderness, a terrifying mountain pass, or royal persecution— and so forth; for by reciting this mantra seven times over earth taken from the horn of a bull while lifting it toward the sky, one shall take hold of the earth of the atmosphere.

In forest wildernesses, on roads, and in royal palaces, no calamities whatsoever shall occur. One should perform this ritual while assuming the form of an elephant-faced one; having placed that earth in one's hand, if it is scattered during a hailstorm and the like, it will be averted—such is the ritual for this.
This is it. [This is the ritual procedure for Gomukha. By means of his hand-claws, he holds back wind, rain, hailstones, and the like.
By this ritual: Oṃ jivili ava avijji sustithada si | isu bhade subhade o | soṇa o acalahi sunnapadani | isila.

*Vadavara ṣa vajrahi svāhā*. Having poured water into a good vessel (*śubhe bhājane udakaṃ dattvā*), and having covered it in a suitable place (*anukūle sthāne pidhāya*), one consecrates it seven times (*saptābhimantritaṃ*).
Having performed [this], if one throws that water into the sky (*udakam ākāśe kṣipet*), it causes hail,
wind, rain, and so forth to be paralyzed (*śilāvātavarṣādikaṃ stambhayati*).
*Namo 'rhatē bhagavate kṣitigarbharājāya tha*.

MA KE HA THA KA RA LA PŪ (263,3) KE | NI TA SAṂ RU BI TI BHA TU YA | RU DZA RI ṬA RA MA ṬA KU KE TO LI ṬA LU YA | U TAṂ HI ṢTHA LI KA RA LE LO HI GRĀ LE BHI ṢI LE ṆA SI MU LE KHA A YA THE SARVVA HATE SRA NA BHU DZ KU ||

*Bhana susthira samaṇapayati śuddhayanaśopadyati taksusala lakhasesi siddhabahālasahi pana svāhā.* If one recites this seven times and washes the face with water, everything will be accomplished. (*udakaṃ*)

Having consecrated it seven times and washed one's face, one accomplishes everything. By arranging Heruka and the ḍākinīs upon the petals in their proper order and joining them with the exhalation of breath, there is no doubt that accomplishment will be attained. Furthermore:
In this regard, yogins should focus their minds intensely upon the lotus; they should make the mind free from waves. If one applies the mantra to the female messenger, it will always be accomplished.
Regarding this, the mantrin has no doubt. From the Great Tantra of the Glorious Vajraḍākinī.
This is the third chapter.
Chapter Four begins:
Furthermore,
there are six heroes who are to be laughed at and thoroughly understood.
Because of the union with the six heroines,
each of the locations consists of a syllable;
first, in the heart itself.
The head is said to be the second;
the crown of the head is assigned as the third;
and the armor is the fourth on the shoulders.
Regarding the syllables, it is the fifth;
the sixth is always spoken of as slow.
This is the fourth chapter from the Great Tantra of Śrī Vajraḍāka.
[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars and does not contain content to translate.]
Furthermore, that which is to be explained next is the supreme assembly of the ḍākinīs,
the thorough binding of all ḍākinīs wherein they are pleased.
It is applied to the four abodes of the pretas, or else to the shore of the ocean, or at a crossroads.
One should thoroughly accomplish it and accomplish all the supreme goals. On mountain caves and forest groves, as well as on a solitary tree—
having thoroughly accomplished it at night with a fearless posture— the yogi...
The unsurpassed [yoga-niruttara] will arise; there, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) will dwell forever together with the ḍākinīs—
of this there is no doubt.
This is the fifth chapter from the Great Tantra of the Glorious Vajra Ḍākinī.
I have thoroughly explained the stages of the ritual procedures for prior practice; listen, O Goddess!
A yogin of asceticism should not perform them.
One should not dwell with anyone else; one should not offer even the highest honor to one’s own body,
nor should one treat it with contempt.
View all diverse things as equal in their lack of intrinsic nature;
one should smear oneself with ashes from charcoal and diligently adorn oneself with dust.
The mantrin should not form conceptual constructions regarding what is edible and what is inedible, and so forth; rather,
with whatever flowers are obtained, all of them.
It should always be worn as a garland.
This is the sixth chapter from the Great Tantra of the Glorious Vajraḍāka.
Next,
the collection of rites for the armors shall be explained;
whatever essence exists within the Triple World, [it is here].
If one mixes it with *unmādana* fruit,
it accomplishes everything in an instant; if one proceeds while reciting the armor-mantra, it will cause movement.
Even the gods do not see him;
he has no fear of robbers, tigers, and the like;
and while wearing his armor, he blesses the royal city.
Once entered, even if one desires to remain unseen, having taken up that bliss, one returns to existence;
while moving about as if changing armor,
one becomes rigid and cannot be shaken even by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
One struck by the foot of the mantra recitation shall not be released again.
This is the seventh chapter from the Great Tantra of the Glorious Vajraḍāka.

Next, the ritual application of the root mantra is explained: through the application of the image made from the five meats, all activities are accomplished; [this applies to] all gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, all gandharvas, and the divine realms.
I go by means of universal mindfulness. [I am] one who terrifies the clouds,
causes them to rain, turns them back, dries up the ocean, reverses the flow of rivers, and turns back the senses.
By reciting [the mantra] over a funeral pyre wood as many times as desired,
whoever is struck with it falls down at that very moment. Having completely consecrated a funeral pyre charcoal,
whoever is struck with it seizes raw flesh at that very moment.
This is the eighth chapter from the Great Tantra of the Glorious Vajraḍāka.
Furthermore, what is to be explained next is the conduct of the ḍākinīs,
as well as the hero's heroism and the assumption of [their] attire.
Having been designated as a messenger, the hero should enjoy the beautiful woman; this is the earth.

One should not disparage even slightly what has been spoken by the Buddhas; one should not apply oneself to anything out of anger, nor should one employ it for mantras. This is the eleventh chapter from the Great Tantra of Śrī Vajraḍāka.
I shall explain the *sādhana* of Vajraḍākinī;
listen, O Goddess! (*śṛṇu devi pravakṣyāmi*)
[The Sadhana of Vajraḍāka]:
First, one should meditate upon a corpse itself; [first, one should visualize a dead body].
The wise should know it to be the nature of the dharmadhātu;
above that, the yogin [should practice].
The yogi, standing upon that,
should meditate on the supreme state; he should cultivate the highest goal.
Having arranged the entire reality (*sakalaṃ tattvaṃ*) right there,
in the center of the moon at one's own heart.
[In the center of the moon within one's own heart], from the syllable *oṃ*,
the goddesses are emanated [by those arisen from its rays].
Having prostrated and performed offerings and so forth, they spoke thus:
"First, in the center of a moon disc at the heart..."
In the morning, within the moon at one's own heart,
having clearly visualized a lunar mandala with the syllable A,
upon that—
One should meditate on the syllable HŪṂ; [having visualized a moon disc by means of the letter A, one should contemplate the syllable HŪṂ above it].
Then, having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness,
one should first draw the mandala.
[Afterwards, one should draw the mandala:
four-cornered and having four gates [caturasraṃ caturdvāraṃ].
Likewise, it should be marked with the vajra of space,
and be properly endowed with four threads.
[Endowed with four cords] and beautifully adorned with a garland of silk ribbons (*paṭṭamālāsuśobhitam*).
In all the corners of the maṇḍalas,
marked with vajra-jewels.
[Inlaid with vajra-jewels],
one should mark the lines for the outer perimeter of the maṇḍala (one should delineate the outer maṇḍala).
The wise one should mark the lines;
it is beautified by a garland of wheels.
[The wheel garland is] very beautiful;
inside that as well,
one should draw a lotus of exquisite white color.
In its center, one should draw a very beautiful white-colored lotus; furthermore, upon that—
Above that, likewise another,
red in color and possessing the luster of a lotus (*rakta-padma-samaprabha*).
Surrounded by a garland of lotuses,
the mantra practitioner [should place it] within that as well.

Paṭala 14 begins:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious maṇḍala of the Mothers.

19.1b The entire *sādhana* of all the gods, the specific [practices] of the messengers (*dūtī*), the great spells (*mahāvidyā*) for spirits and seizing demons (*bhūtagraha*), and whoever is the bodily emanation—
And likewise, O goddess, as for the others—the *kaṭapūtanas*—and so forth; thus it has been explained. Now listen, O Goddess, as the *Mantramālā* is being described.

[Square with four gates] | Endowed with gatekeepers [dvārapālasamanvitam] | The foundation of all qualities of accomplishment, one should draw the beautiful mandala [likhen maṇḍalavaraṃ sarvasiddhiguṇālayam].

the wind has a deer for its mount.

possessing miraculous powers and great renown,

I shall explain the *sādhana* of the messenger (*dūtī*),
which is difficult to find within all the tantras.
[Difficult to find in all tantras:
By being endowed with that, siddhi will arise;
by abiding constantly through a single yoga.
One is definitively liberated from the defects of saṃsāra; one is eternally liberated from attachment to female messengers;
one should practice according to the supreme stage.
It is not that one should not offer even mere service; even those of low birth are objects of joy and delight—
mothers, sisters, and daughters.

[The *Śrīvajraḍāka-uttaratantra-sārasaṃgraha*].

This was translated by the great Indian preceptor Paramesvara and the Tibetan monk Śākya Vīrya at the secluded hermitage of Lhari-mo-gu in Grom-pa Rulag-rgyang-phu.

This is the only instance in the text where the name *Vajraḍākottara* appears; all the preceding chapters (*paṭalas*) state that they belong to the *Vajraḍāka*, with the exception of one chapter which claims to be from the *Vajraḍākinītantra* (likely a later interpolation).
[This is likely] a scribal error. Therefore, one may question the attribution of this title to the entire work.
